seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: I have received just this moment your note with enclosures from Mr Yeats, Mr Gosse and Mr Wells. I owe these last two gentlemen a letter of thanks for the kind interest they seem to take in me – but especially to yourself and Yeats. Here are the facts of the case which Mr Gosse asks for.

I am here (at this new address) with wife and children – two, aged ten and eight. For the last six months I have had great difficulty in living. In order to leave Trieste I had to raise money on my furniture. The fare and other expenses here brought that supply to an end. I have of course no means of support though I am looking for lessons every day. (LII 352).
… I have received a small amount of money from a connection of mine by marriage and it is this at present which keeps me and my family. I cannot count on any definite supply from that source as he has his own family and is not rich. (LII 352-53). If there be any such fund as that you write of and if its committee consider my case favourably I beg you to let me know. I suppose I shall receive nothing in the way of royalties. (LII 353). I thought of sending two or three verses to Mr Pinker but even that would not mend matters much. Perhaps when the scholastic year begins again in October I can find some kind of teaching here in Switzerland – either in Zurich or in French Switzerland. This is my hope as I am afraid (LII 353).
… I cannot go back to Trieste for some time to come. (LII 353). If I may be allowed to say so I should prefer the matter to proceed along this line rather than along that so kindly suggested by Mr Wells and Mr Hueffer . I am sure it will be possible to find some such position here (my ambition is not high) especially if I know where to apply. I must tell you that travelling at present (in the condition in which we find ourselves, physically and morally) is to be avoided if possible. Although the prospect is rather cloudy (or seemed to be until your letter arrived) we are at least safe. The last raid of Italian airships (as I read) was directed against the Trieste shipyard – about five minutes from my house. (LII 353).

I brought with me the MS of my play. I am trying to get it typed at once. As Mr Gosse seems to wish to read some of my writing perhaps it would be well to send him the first chapters of my novel. It began on 2 Feby February 1914. As you think best, however. I am afraid that I give everybody a great deal of trouble.

I received a form to fill up for Who’s Who? : and sent it on. I suspect that there must be some reader of The Egoist or some friend of yours in the publishing office. Otherwise I cannot explain in view of the fact that the two books which I have written and published have fallen stillborn from the press.
I shall not bore you by writing any more. I suppose I have given you the facts of the case. They reduce themselves to one very simple fact.

Many sincere thanks to Yeats and yourself for your active friendship (in the name also of the three other beneficiaries presumptive) and may I add a word of thanks also to Mrs Pound for her flattering opinion of my stories?

div.note: Typed excerpts from this letter were included in LII 352-53 and dated “about 15 July 1915.” The original letter is clearly dated by Joyce as 14 July 1915.
JJ and his family moved to 7 Reinhardstrasse from Gasthof Hoffnung circa 7 July 1915 and stayed in “rooms” there until 15 October, “not knowing where else to go or what to do” (LII 351).
Pound’s short letter to JJ with enclosures was sent circa 10 July 1915 (Pound/Joyce 36-37).

Pound made great efforts to obtain a grant for JJ from the Royal Literary Fund, founded in 1790 to assist British writers in financial straits. Pound wrote H.G. Wells (1866-1946) on JJ’s behalf, and got W.B. Yeats to approach the English author Edmund Gosse (1849-1928), an official of the Fund. Yeats assured the Fund of his belief that JJ was “a man of genius” with “a most beautiful gift,” and “the most remarkable new talent in Ireland today” (Ellmann, JJ 390-91). The Fund awarded JJ £75, payable in three installments over nine months; he received the first installment of £25 on 31 August 1915 (LII 362-63).
J.B. Pinker, JJ’s London literary agent. See JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes. For the poems JJ eventually placed in Poetry magazine for May 1917, see JJ to Pound, 10 March 1916, notes.

Wells wrote Pound that the English writer Ford Madox Hueffer (1873-1939) had said he could get JJ a job in the War Office working in the censorship department (Pound/Joyce 37). JJ preferred, however, to teach English as he had been doing in Trieste, both at the Scuola Superiore di Commercio Revoltella and in private lessons.

In his letter to JJ of 3 July 1915, Pound wrote that an “American agent for a large theatre co.” had promised to read JJ’s play Exiles (Pound/Joyce 36). JJ had the play typed from manuscript in exchange for English lessons, and forwarded its three acts to his literary agent J.B. Pinker in three separate mailings, to minimize the risk of postal mishap (LII 353). Pinker sent the play to Cecil I. Dorrian (1882-1926), a female American journalist and war correspondent who also acted as European agent for Oliver Morosco (1875-1945), a theatrical impresario based in Los Angeles who produced plays there and in New York City. In August 1915, Pinker informed JJ that Dorrian had a “good opinion” of Exiles but felt she had to turn it down as “unfit for her theatre” (LII 363).

Pound’s letter to JJ of circa 10 July 1915 contained a letter from Gosse to Yeats, dated 7 July 1915, in which Gosse expressed willingness to help JJ with the Royal Literary Fund and asked for “some account of his works, for I am ashamed to say I know nothing of them” (Pound/Joyce 37). A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was published serially in the London magazine, The Egoist, beginning 2 February 1914, JJ’s thirty-second birthday. Whatever Gosse’s views of JJ’s early work, he detested Ulysses as “an anarchical production, infamous in taste, in style, in everything.” JJ was “a sort of Marquis de Sade,” Gosse thought, “but does not write so well” (Ellmann, JJ 528 n.).

JJ described himself in the Who’s Who entry form as “teacher of the Scuola Superiore di Commercio, Trieste, and writer.” The fifteen-line entry as printed stated, inaccurately, that he had married Nora Barnacle in 1904, and gave his publications as Chamber Music, Dubliners, A Portrait, and contributions to Fortnightly Review, Saturday Review, Speaker, Smart Set, The Egoist, and Piccolo della Sera. His recreation was listed as “singing” (Who’s Who 1916 [London: A&C Black Ltd.], 1206).

JJ’s volume of poems, Chamber Music, published by Elkin Mathews in 1907, was praised by Yeats and Arthur Symons but never earned JJ royalties. Dubliners, too, had yet to bring JJ any earnings at this time.

Pound’s wife Dorothy, née Shakespear (1886-1973), had remarked after reading JJ’s stories for the second time, “They are excellently good, aren’t they,” as Pound reported to JJ circa June 1915 (Pound/Joyce 35). She later admired Ulysses and recommended it to her son in 1946 as “a demonic book, of real value [with] all the greatness due to tremendous form, inside its frame (24. hrs of Dublin.)” (Ezra and Dorothy Pound: Letters in Captivity, 1945-1946, ed. Omar Pound and Robert Spoo [New York: Oxford University Press, 1999], 265).
